front.title: Service Orchestration with YANG-modeled Abstractions Framework

abstract.t: This document defines the Service Orchestration with YANG-modeled Abstractions (SOYA) Framework for building layered orchestration systems using YANG models, and specifies the interactions between different orchestration layers.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: The YANG Data Modeling Language () has become ubiquitous in modern network management and is widely adopted for modeling configuration and state data for network devices. YANG equally lends itself to describing higher-level orchestration intent at various layers of abstraction.

This document defines the Service Orchestration with YANG-modeled Abstractions (SOYA) Framework for building layered orchestration systems. Each layer allows for the expression of a service intent, according to a set of YANG models. These layers may be hosted on separate SOYA Orchestrators or within a single SOYA Orchestrator, depending on the deployment architecture.

Service intent, e.g. configuration, flows from the highest abstraction layer down to the managed devices. Operational state, on the other hand, flows from the devices up to the higher abstraction layers. The framework specifies permissible data exchanges between different abstraction layers, both within a single SOYA Orchestrator and across multiple SOYA Orchestrators.

section.name: Definition of SOYA Orchestrator
section.t: In the context of this document, a SOYA Orchestrator refers to a software component responsible for managing network services by processing service intent and operational state. A variety of terms exist in the industry, including domain orchestrator, network orchestrator, domain controller, and SDN controller. Any platform capable of adhering to the SOYA framework, can be referred to as a SOYA Orchestrator.

section.name: The SOYA Orchestrator
section.t: A SOYA Orchestrator is a software component capable of receiving, storing, and processing service intent. In a SOYA Orchestrator, intent is stored in a datastore as defined in . SOYA Orchestrators must implement, at a minimum, the <running-config> datastore as defined in .

Processing each received intent update involves executing the SOYA Orchestrator's business logic for that layer. The business logic is responsible for producing an output intent for the next layer down; or forthe managed device(s) in case of the lowest service layer.

The SOYA Orchestrator may also support receiving/collecting operational state from its managed devices or from other service layers. Processing a received operational state update involves analyzing it according to its business logic and determining the necessary actions. Those may include updating the SOYA Orchestrator's internal state, generating new service intents for the lower layer, or triggering specific configuration changes on managed devices. The SOYA Orchestrator can also propagate operational state updates to the next orchestration layer up, generate notifications, or raise alarms.

section.name: Single-Layer Orchestrator
section.t: A single-layer SOYA Orchestrator stores and processes service intents and operational state at a specific layer of abstraction. It processes service intents and operational state relevant to its layer and interacts with both the higher orchestration layer (if any) and the lower orchestration layer or managed devices.

section.name: Multi-Layer Orchestrator
section.t: A multi-layer SOYA Orchestrator is capable of storing and processing service intents and operational state on multiple layers of abstraction within a single orchestrator instance. The orchestrator must ensure that the layering principles as described in are adhered to for each individual abstraction layer that it hosts.

In a multi-layer SOYA Orchestrator, the implementation must be written such that proper layering and separation of concerns are maintained at all times. Each individual layer must be thought of as its own YANG datastore in its own namespace. As an intent update triggers the business logic on a particular layer, that layer's business logic must only access (read) intent data (configuration) within its own layer. The business logic may produce an update to the configuration on the layer just below it as described in .

section.name: Service Layering
section.t: An overall orchestration system may be comprised of multiple layers, each responsible for a specific level of abstraction in managing network services. The schema for each layer is defined by a set of YANG models. All YANG validation is performed within the context of the specific layer's schema. A YANG module from one layers cannot import modules from another layer, XPath expressions may only refer to nodes within the same layer, etc.

section.name: Propagating Service Intent Down
section.t: Outside intent configuration (i.e., configuration originating from outside the orchestration system) enters the orchestration system at the top-most service layer only. For this purpose, top-most layer must be exposed through one or more northbound interfaces []. It is then propagated down through the layers, with each layer's business logic translating the intent into the appropriate configuration for the layer below.

The orchestrator(s) hosting the lower layer(s) must be configured to only accept and apply the configuration updates generated by the layer above. The configuration of the lower layers may be exposed to outside observers in a read-only manner, they should not be allowed to modify it.

The lowest service layer's business logic is responsible for generating the actual device configuration according to the YANG models the managed device(s) support over the available southbound interfaces [].

section.name: Propagating Operational State Up
section.t: The business logic at each layer is responsible for maintaining and publishing its own operational state information as "config false" YANG modeled data.

While in the SOYA architecture, it is permissible for the business logic at any layer to read the operational state information from anywhere in the stack, the best practice is for operational state to flow up, layer by layer.

For example, when a device publishes its operational state updates, they are collected and processed by the business logic at the lowest abstraction layer. That layer may then publish updates to its own operational state information, which is consumed by the layer above and so forth up the stack. This pattern simplifies the business logic at the higher layers, as they only need to deal with the abstracted operational state rather than the raw device-level details.

section.name: SAIN Integration
section.t: The Service Assurance for Intent-Based Networking (SAIN) orchestrator defined in could be integrated with a SOYA Orchestrator to derive an assurance graph from service intent and the corresponding configuration generated for lower layers and devices. The SAIN orchestrator would configure SAIN agents using the YANG modules defined in to monitor the services and their dependencies.

The resulting health scores and symptoms, gathered by a SAIN collector, could be fed back to the business logic at the relevant SOYA layer. That layer would map these results to its own service instances and publish the appropriate "config false" operational state for broader consumption. This allows SAIN to provide service assurance while each SOYA layer retains responsibility for the operational state it exposes.
